A Zurich police task force, which includes an art expert, had received tips from around the world, police said. The task force was looking into possible connections with other art thefts inside Switzerland and abroad. The director of the Kunsthaus serves on the E.G. Buhrle private art foundation's council, Quellenberg said. # Two Zurich Masterpieces Found Days After $163 Million Heist; Cézanne Recovered Four Years Later

**ZURICH —** Four paintings by some of Europe’s most celebrated artists were taken at gunpoint from Zurich’s E.G. Bührle Collection in February 2008, setting off an international investigation that produced a quick, unexpected breakthrough, followed by years of painstaking police work.

The robbery occurred on **Sunday, February 10, 2008**, and was announced publicly the following day. The four works—then valued together at about **180 million Swiss francs, or $163 million**—were:

- Paul Cézanne’s *The Boy in the Red Vest*  
- Edgar Degas’s *Count Lepic and His Daughters*  
- Claude Monet’s *Poppies near Vétheuil*  
- Vincent van Gogh’s *Blossoming Chestnut Branches*

## Armed raid in broad daylight

According to Swiss police, three masked men entered the museum shortly before closing time. At least one carried a handgun. The robbers forced staff and visitors to the floor, removed the four paintings from the gallery and fled in a waiting vehicle.

The thieves appeared to have selected highly recognizable works, but that created an immediate problem: paintings of such fame and value are almost impossible to sell openly. Their images were rapidly distributed to police forces, customs agencies, auction houses and art dealers around the world.

Authorities announced a reward and appealed for witnesses, while the museum temporarily closed and reviewed its security arrangements. Investigators examined whether the thieves were experienced art criminals, acting on commission, or opportunists who had underestimated how difficult it would be to dispose of the pictures.

## Monet and van Gogh found in an unlocked car

Eight days after the robbery, on **February 18**, police recovered the Monet and van Gogh in a parked, unlocked car in Zurich, only a short distance from the museum. The vehicle was near the grounds of the Burghölzli psychiatric hospital.

The two paintings were visible inside the car and were retrieved without a confrontation. Specialists subsequently confirmed that they were the stolen originals. Officials said the works were in generally good condition, although they were examined carefully for damage caused by their hasty removal and inadequate storage.

The recovery immediately raised questions. Investigators considered whether the robbers had abandoned the pictures because of the intense publicity, whether the car had been intended as a temporary hiding place, or whether the works were left as part of an attempted negotiation. Police released few operational details, saying that doing so could jeopardize the search for the thieves and the other paintings.

The recovered works were returned to the Bührle collection after forensic and conservation examinations. Security was strengthened before they were displayed again.

## Investigation spreads across Europe

The Cézanne and Degas remained missing, and the case moved into the international art-crime network. Swiss authorities worked with Interpol and police agencies elsewhere in Europe. Investigators monitored possible ransom approaches and efforts to use the paintings as collateral in criminal transactions.

Experts noted that stolen masterpieces often remain hidden for years. Rather than being sold to a secret collector, they may be traded within criminal circles, pledged against debts or offered back to insurers and owners through intermediaries.

For a long period, authorities reported no public breakthrough. The investigation nevertheless remained active, with intelligence eventually leading toward the Balkans.

## Cézanne recovered in Serbia

In **April 2012**, more than four years after the Zurich robbery, Serbian police recovered Cézanne’s *The Boy in the Red Vest* during an operation in and around Belgrade. Several suspects were arrested.

Serbian officials said the suspects had been attempting to obtain millions of euros for the painting. Police also seized cash, vehicles and weapons during the operation. The recovery followed cooperation between Serbian and Swiss authorities and an investigation that reportedly involved controlled contacts with people seeking to sell or ransom the work.

The canvas was initially examined in Serbia and later authenticated as the Cézanne stolen from Zurich. It was eventually returned to the Bührle collection. The painting was the most valuable of the four works, having been estimated at roughly **100 million Swiss francs** at the time of the theft.

The Serbian arrests also gave investigators their strongest opportunity to reconstruct the robbery and the later movement of the stolen art. Authorities examined whether those arrested had participated directly in the Zurich raid or had acquired the Cézanne later through criminal intermediaries. Not all details of the investigation or the suspects’ respective roles were made public.

## Degas remains the unresolved part of the case

The recovery of the Cézanne meant that three of the four stolen paintings had been found. The Degas, *Count Lepic and His Daughters*, remained missing in the last widely reported official accounts of the case.

Its absence left several central questions unanswered: whether it followed the same route as the Cézanne, whether it was transferred to another criminal group, or whether it was concealed separately soon after the robbery.

The Zurich theft became one of the most prominent examples of the contradictions surrounding high-value art crime. The robbers succeeded in removing works worth an extraordinary sum, but the paintings’ fame made them liabilities almost immediately. Two were abandoned within days, a third surfaced only after four years and an international police operation, and the fourth disappeared into the illicit market.

The E.G. Bührle Collection, assembled by Swiss industrialist Emil Georg Bührle, later moved its public presentation to the Kunsthaus Zürich. The heist nevertheless remains a major episode in the history of the collection—and an investigation that cannot be considered fully closed while the Degas is still unaccounted for.

# The 2008 Zurich Art Heist: Armed Robbery at the Bührle Collection

On February 10, 2008, three armed men entered the E. G. Bührle Collection in Zurich and stole four major Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings. Valued together at roughly **180 million Swiss francs—about US$160–165 million at the time—the theft was described as one of the largest art robberies in European history**.

Two paintings were recovered within days, a third was found in Serbia four years later, and the fourth—Edgar Degas’s *Ludovic Lepic and His Daughters*—remains publicly listed as missing.

## The Bührle Collection

The Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection occupied a villa in Zurich’s Seefeld district. Its holdings were assembled by Emil Georg Bührle, an industrialist and arms manufacturer whose collecting activities and wartime business dealings have generated substantial historical controversy. The collection nevertheless contained an exceptional group of works by artists including Cézanne, Degas, Monet, Renoir and Van Gogh.

At the time of the robbery, the museum was relatively small and lacked the physical security of a large national institution. Visitors could approach many of the paintings closely, and the thieves selected four especially recognizable works hanging in the same room.

## The four stolen paintings

Estimates varied among police, insurers and news organizations, and the figures were never formal sale prices. The values most often reported were:

| Artist and work | Date | Approximate reported value | Status |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Paul Cézanne, *The Boy in the Red Vest***, also translated as *The Boy in the Red Waistcoat* | c. 1888–1890 or 1894–1895, depending on cataloguing | About **100 million Swiss francs** | Recovered in Serbia in 2012 |
| **Claude Monet, *Poppies near Vétheuil*** | 1879 | Often estimated at roughly **50–70 million Swiss francs** | Recovered in Zurich in February 2008 |
| **Vincent van Gogh, *Blossoming Chestnut Branches*** | 1890 | Often estimated at roughly **15–20 million Swiss francs**, though some contemporary reports used higher figures | Recovered in Zurich in February 2008 |
| **Edgar Degas, *Ludovic Lepic and His Daughters***, also called *Count Lepic and His Daughters* | c. 1871 | Commonly estimated at about **10 million Swiss francs** | Still missing |

The frequently quoted total was **180 million Swiss francs**. Individual valuations reported at the time were inconsistent, so they should be treated as approximate insurance or press estimates rather than proven market values.

## How the robbery happened

The raid took place late on a Sunday afternoon, shortly before the museum was due to close.

According to police accounts:

1. **Three masked men entered the museum**, at least one carrying a handgun.
2. One robber **fired a shot into the air or ceiling** to intimidate staff and visitors.
3. People inside were ordered to lie on the floor.
4. While one man controlled the room, the others removed the four paintings from the walls.
5. The robbers carried the canvases outside and escaped in a waiting vehicle, widely described as a **white car**.

The operation lasted only a few minutes. No one was physically injured, although visitors and employees were threatened at gunpoint.

The choice of paintings appeared opportunistic as well as deliberate. All four were extremely valuable, but they were also close together and could be removed quickly. Their fame made them virtually impossible to sell openly, a recurring problem in high-profile art theft: celebrated works may have enormous theoretical value but almost no legitimate resale market.

There were also indications that the thieves had difficulty transporting all four canvases. The paintings recovered days later were found in a car not far from the museum, suggesting that the group may have abandoned part of the haul because of police pressure, logistical problems, or fear that possession of the best-known works would expose them.

## Immediate police response

Zurich police launched a major investigation as soon as the alarm was raised. The response included:

- Road checks and searches for the getaway vehicle;
- Alerts to Swiss border authorities and police agencies abroad;
- Distribution of photographs and descriptions through international art-crime channels, including Interpol;
- Interviews with museum staff, visitors and nearby residents;
- Examination of physical evidence and available surveillance material;
- Appeals to the public for information; and
- A reward, initially reported as **100,000 Swiss francs**, for information leading to the paintings’ return.

Because the robbery occurred in a city close to several national borders and involved portable objects that could quickly be moved by road, Swiss investigators immediately treated international trafficking as a strong possibility.

## Two paintings found in an abandoned car

On February 18, eight days after the robbery, police announced the recovery of the Monet and Van Gogh.

The two paintings were discovered in a parked car near the **Burghölzli psychiatric hospital**, only a short distance from the Bührle museum. They were lying in the vehicle and could reportedly be seen from outside. Police secured the car and had the works authenticated.

The recovered paintings were:

- Claude Monet’s *Poppies near Vétheuil*; and
- Vincent van Gogh’s *Blossoming Chestnut Branches*.

Both were reported to be in reasonably good condition, although they underwent professional examination for damage caused by hurried removal, handling and storage.

The location was strikingly close to the scene of the crime. Investigators considered whether the thieves had intended to retrieve the paintings later, whether an accomplice had failed to collect them, or whether they had been deliberately abandoned once the scale of the police operation became clear. No definitive public explanation was established.

## Recovery of Cézanne’s *The Boy in the Red Vest*

The most valuable stolen work, Cézanne’s *The Boy in the Red Vest*, remained missing until April 2012.

Serbian police, working with Swiss authorities, recovered the painting during an operation centered on Belgrade. Investigators said suspects had attempted to arrange an illicit sale of the Cézanne for only a small fraction of its estimated value—reports commonly cited an asking price of about **€3.5 million**, despite the work’s valuation of approximately 100 million Swiss francs.

Several suspects were arrested in Serbia. Police also reported seizing cash, weapons and ammunition. The painting was authenticated and eventually returned to the Bührle Foundation.

The recovery demonstrated a familiar pattern in major art thefts: a masterpiece that cannot be sold through legitimate channels circulates in the criminal underground, where it may be offered as collateral, used in attempted bargaining, or sold at a steep discount to buyers who know it is stolen.

Authorities linked the Serbian suspects to the Zurich robbery, but not every detail of the operation—including who planned the raid, who entered the museum and how the painting traveled from Switzerland to the Balkans—was made fully public.

## The Degas remains missing

Degas’s *Ludovic Lepic and His Daughters* was not recovered with the Monet and Van Gogh in 2008 or with the Cézanne in 2012.

The painting portrays Degas’s friend Ludovic-Napoléon Lepic with his daughters. Though assigned the lowest monetary estimate of the four stolen works, it remains historically and artistically significant.

Its fate is unknown. Possibilities include concealment in a private location, movement through criminal networks, damage or destruction, or an attempted secret sale. No verified public evidence has established where it is.

## Possible connection to other Swiss art thefts

The Bührle robbery occurred amid several prominent art crimes in Switzerland, prompting investigators and the press to ask whether the cases were connected.

### The Picasso theft at Pfäffikon

Only days before the Zurich raid, on February 6, 2008, two paintings by Pablo Picasso were stolen from an exhibition at the Seedamm Culture Centre in Pfäffikon, canton Schwyz. The works, on loan from the Sprengel Museum in Hanover, were:

- *Tête de cheval*—*Head of a Horse*; and
- *Verre et pichet*—*Glass and Pitcher*.

Their combined value was reported at several million Swiss francs or dollars.

The closeness in time and geography made a connection with the Bührle robbery an obvious line of inquiry. Both cases involved famous, difficult-to-sell works taken from relatively small Swiss exhibition venues. Nevertheless, the methods differed: the Bührle theft was a brazen armed robbery during opening hours, while the Picasso theft was carried out under different circumstances. No conclusive public evidence established that the same group was responsible.

The two Picassos were eventually recovered in Serbia in 2011, adding to suspicions that stolen Western European art was moving through Balkan criminal networks. The following year, the stolen Cézanne was also found in Serbia. That geographic overlap suggested common trafficking routes or contacts, but it did not by itself prove that the original thefts had been organized by the same people.

### Broader regional pattern

Switzerland’s location, wealth, private collections and proximity to multiple borders have long made it attractive to art criminals. The country also experienced other thefts from museums, exhibitions, galleries and private collections.

Investigators considered whether the Bührle robbery involved an established international gang, including networks operating in southeastern Europe. Comparisons were sometimes made with the so-called **Pink Panthers**, a loose label applied to Balkan-linked jewel thieves and other organized-crime figures. Publicly available evidence, however, has not conclusively attributed the Zurich raid to that organization.

It is therefore most accurate to say:

- The Bührle robbery and other Swiss thefts occurred in a similar period;
- Some stolen works from separate cases surfaced in Serbia;
- Investigators examined possible links and shared trafficking channels;
- But no single, fully proven conspiracy connecting all the thefts has been publicly demonstrated.

## Why the case mattered

The heist exposed the vulnerability of small museums holding extremely valuable works. A few armed men were able to overpower staff, remove four paintings and escape within minutes. Afterward, the Bührle Foundation closed temporarily and reviewed its security arrangements.

The case also illustrated the paradox of stolen masterpieces. Their public value is immense, yet their notoriety makes legal sale almost impossible. Recovery may depend on years of surveillance, informants, undercover negotiations and cooperation across national borders.

As of the publicly known record, three of the four works have returned:

- Monet’s *Poppies near Vétheuil* — recovered in 2008;
- Van Gogh’s *Blossoming Chestnut Branches* — recovered in 2008;
- Cézanne’s *The Boy in the Red Vest* — recovered in Serbia in 2012.

Degas’s *Ludovic Lepic and His Daughters* remains the unresolved element of one of Europe’s most spectacular modern art heists.
